body: ONLY IF PEOPLE ARE ON SCREEN: CANDID, NOT ACTED: reactions are small and real, like a phone video of real people – a quick surprised blink, a pause, a half laugh, eyebrows up, an eye-roll – never cartoon faces (no saucer-round eyes, no mouth held wide open, no frozen grimace). No expression is held longer than about 1.5 s; the face keeps changing with breath and thought. Skin stays real while moving: pores, fine lines, small blemishes, a little shine, uneven tone – no beauty filter, no airbrushed or waxy smoothing. Every action is done by the person it was written for (name them by position and clothes) – never swap who does what.

ONLY IF PEOPLE ARE IN THE PICTURE: CANDID, NOT POSED: a real moment caught by a camera – a natural half smile, a glance to the side, a word in mid-sentence, relaxed hands – never a frozen grin, saucer-round eyes or a cartoon face. Real skin: pores, fine lines, small blemishes, a little shine, uneven tone, stray hairs – no beauty filter, no airbrushed or waxy smoothing, no glow. Eyes with catch-lights and one believable focus point. Each person does exactly what was asked of them (name them by position and clothes) – never swap who holds or does what.

LIQUID SPILLED ON A SURFACE: first a visible continuous stream from the container to the surface, then the impact splash with flying droplets, then the puddle keeps spreading and thinning for seconds, following the slope; edges are irregular and wet-shiny (never a crisp star-shaped decal that stops moving). It flows around and soaks into what lies in it (a pile of coffee grounds darkens, turns into wet sludge and smears), runs over the edge in drips, and leaves small splatter on nearby objects, hands and clothes. The container loses exactly as much as is spilled; a stream aimed into a cup ends in the cup.

POWDER OR GRAINS FROM A SPOON: the grains are SEEN falling in a short stream from the tipped spoon to the surface, with a small puff of dust on impact; the pile is loose and uneven with stray grains around it (never a neat moulded dome); the spoon is empty afterwards and has to be filled again before the next drop; the pile only grows when more is visibly added, and it keeps its exact place.

FOOD TIPPED OUT OF A POT OR PAN: the lid is visibly taken off first (or slides off and clatters into the sink – it never just vanishes); the food slides out in clumps following gravity, lands loosely and spreads, some grains stick to the pot and the sink walls, hot food steams. It never forms a perfect dome and it never appears in the sink without being seen falling.

HOT COOKWARE AND KITCHEN TEXTILES: a hot pot or pan is held by its handles with a folded kitchen towel or oven mitts, people keep it away from the body and flinch from the steam when the lid opens; the lid has a knob and stays a separate object that is put down somewhere visible. A kitchen towel stays the same thin cotton towel (same colour and size) when it is picked up, swung or thrown; mitts are taken off before the hands do something else.

REAL PHONE HOME VIDEO: one continuous take, as if filmed on a phone – either propped on a shelf (almost still, a tiny wobble, slight auto-exposure and focus breathing) or held by hand (gentle sway); no cuts between wide and close shots, no zooms or cinematic moves unless asked. Ordinary home light from the ceiling lamps and windows, natural colours, slight sensor grain and mild compression, a little noise in the shadows; no film grading, no studio light, no glow. People behave as if nobody is filming; at most a short glance at the phone.

DISTRACTED PEOPLE: state exactly where each person looks and keep it – their eyes stay locked on what distracts them (the TV, a phone) for the whole action, with small reactions to it (smile, nod, raised eyebrow); they do NOT look at each other or at their hands unless the plan says so. The hands work by feel – reaching, searching, missing by a few centimetres. Only when the mistake is complete do they look down, with one beat of realisation.

A TV PLAYING OFF-SCREEN: its sound is thin and boxy (little bass), with the room's echo, quieter than the people in the room and it dips whenever someone speaks; a news bulletin is a formal Arabic anchor voice with a short breaking-news sting. The TV light flickers softly on the faces and the wall facing it in changing cool tones; the screen itself stays out of frame unless asked.

REAL-LIFE COMEDY: a simple, clear setup; the joke happens fully visible in frame (the miss, the spill, the fall) with real cause and effect; timing is action – one beat of silence – realisation – the punchline line – a small reaction (eye-roll, shrug, half laugh). Performances stay natural and underplayed, nobody mugs at the camera; the funny part is the situation, not exaggerated faces.

INDOORS AT HOME, WHAT LOOKS MOST REAL: bright soft daylight from a window (evening rooms and warm lamps look staged), a phone standing on the table or counter, slightly low, facing the people, and staying completely still for the whole take. People are big in frame, upper bodies and both faces clearly visible, with a few simple everyday objects around them. Avoid wide shots of a whole room and tidy showroom rooms. Do not ask for a slow push-in or a camera move here: it tends to turn into hard cuts.

A SHORT CLIP HOLDS ONE THING: about 12 seconds carries one main action and two or three short spoken lines, no more. Write it as 6–7 plain beats with their seconds, one clear action per beat and who does it, in simple words. Short plain beats work better than long lists of physics rules. Everything else is left out: fewer people, fewer objects, fewer moves. The scene must already be right in the first frame, so a real, sharp start picture matters more than any later wording.

KEEPING A REAL PERSON'S FACE: a face holds best looking towards the camera, big in frame, with few people around. Turned heads, profiles and group shots change the face most, so give them only short moments and return to the front. Copy the person from the reference photo, not the logos or printed words on their clothes or behind them: state that those are left out. Keep their own skin as it is in the photo – add no acne, spots, red patches or scars they do not have.

IF ANYONE SPEAKS: give each line word for word, with who says it and to whom, because Iraqi words change with the person addressed (شبيك to a man, شبيچ to a woman). Only those lines are spoken: nobody repeats a line, adds a word or shouts something extra. One speaker at a time, with a short pause between turns. A laugh comes before or after a line as its own beat, never inside the same breath as the words.

A THIEF OR MASKED MAN IN A COMEDY SKIT: he comes in, makes ONE quick grab of something already within reach (one stack of notes, one bag) and leaves. Several grabs, big piles and slow searching look staged. He moves like a nervous ordinary person, fast and a little clumsy, with no film-villain poses. The people in the room react small and slightly late. It stays a joke: nobody is hurt, no blood.

MONEY AND OTHER SMALL THINGS IN HANDS: keep the number low and say it ("only one stack", "two stacks"). When many items are picked up or moved they float, multiply or vanish. Each item is seen being picked up, stays in the hand that took it, and the place it came from is visibly emptier afterwards.

A TV IN THE SHOT: a visible screen tends to freeze into a still picture, which gives the shot away. Unless the screen itself is the point, place the TV out of frame behind the phone, so the people look past the camera at it and its light and sound tell the story. If the screen must show, the picture on it keeps visibly moving and changing the whole time.

HANDS UP IN SHOCK: the hands go up fast and uneven, one higher than the other, never tidy and equal. Say at which second they come down and when the person turns; left unsaid, the hands stay up stiffly to the end of the clip.

WHISPERING OR LEANING IN CLOSE: the lips stop a clear hand's width away from the ear and the cheek, with a hand cupped beside the mouth, and the head moves back afterwards. If the lips reach the temple or cheek it reads as a kiss.
